learningObjective: Distinguish latency from throughput and identify architectural strategies that optimize one at the expense of the other.
stem: Which of the following correctly distinguish latency from throughput in an architectural context? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Latency and throughput are reciprocals of each other, so improving one automatically improves the other by the same factor.

A workload's latency floor is at least the longest sequential dependency chain; increasing parallelism reduces throughput bottlenecks but cannot shrink an unavoidable data dependency's contribution to latency.

Latency is the time to complete one unit of work end-to-end; throughput is the rate of completed work per unit time. On pipelined or heavily parallel systems, throughput can be high while individual latency remains long.
GPU architectures optimize primarily for throughput via massive parallelism and latency hiding through overlapping many warps, at the cost of higher per-op latency than a CPU on isolated operations.

explanation: A: Textbook definition and the observation that pipelined systems trade single-item latency for aggregate throughput. B: GPUs use SIMT with many warps and latency-hiding memory pipelines; single-issue latency on a CPU is often lower for a lone dependent instruction stream. D: Sequential dependencies (critical path) bound latency; parallelism can widen the pipeline but cannot fold two dependent ops in half. C is wrong: latency and throughput are not reciprocals when pipelining or parallelism is involved; throughput can be N-way while per-item latency is still 1 unit of pipeline depth.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: they are not simple reciprocals; pipelining and parallelism decouple them.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: critical path (sequential dependencies) sets a latency floor even with unlimited workers.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: standard definitions with the pipeline caveat.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical characterization of GPU throughput orientation vs CPU latency orientation.

assumptions: Comparison of GPUs and CPUs as throughput- vs latency-oriented, respectively, per architectural design goals.
The workload can be pipelined or parallelized; a purely sequential critical-path workload is not the general case.
nonImplications: Does not imply CPUs are always slower per-op than GPUs; per-thread latency on CPUs is often lower for scalar workloads.
Does not imply throughput and latency are unrelated; they are related by Little's Law, but not as simple reciprocals.

distractorRationales.A: Overly simple algebraic relation that ignores pipelining and parallelism.
